answer:
The biggest exposure here is that a single rotating mechanism design, qualified once and repeated across several programmes and both flight units, is being flown with almost no spares margin and under schedule pressure on a supplier-built unit — any defect that escapes acceptance testing is likely to be common to both strings and to sister missions.

### 1. Common defect undetected because the qualification/verification method had no independent check
Two identical cross-strapped units built to one heritage standard and tested by one method share whatever blind spot that method has — redundancy only helps if the failure modes are independent. The precedent is the Hubble primary mirror, ground to a precise but wrong figure because the reflective null corrector used to verify it was never cross-checked by an independent technique; the error was reproduced on every measurement that used the same corrector. The Board stressed that a single, uncorroborated test method is not sufficient verification for a critical, unrepairable optical or mechanical figure. [The Hubble Space Telescope Optical Systems Failure Report](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19910003124/downloads/19910003124.pdf#page=31)

Check: confirm the prism figure, bearing preload setup, and encoder calibration were each verified by at least one method independent of the primary production test rig, for both flight units.

### 2. Inadequate independent oversight of a supplier building to heritage standard
Work done by a subcontractor on a critical, schedule-pressured item can proceed with QA effectively locked out — access restricted, paperwork not filed, discrepant data never escalated — so a flaw is only found after the hardware is on orbit. The investigators called for QA to have full, independent access from conception to delivery, authority to stop work, and a reporting path insulated from programme schedule pressure. [The Hubble Space Telescope Optical Systems Failure Report](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19910003124/downloads/19910003124.pdf#page=52)

Check: verify the horizon sensor supplier's QA has unrestricted access and documented sign-off on bearing preload, lubrication, and encoder alignment steps, independent of program cost/schedule pressure.

### 3. Unrecertified material or process substitution under a heritage build standard
A long-flying heritage design invites small vendor-level substitutions (lubricant, elastomer, potting compound) that are never flagged up the chain. In one case a vendor substituted a certified material in a flight battery relief valve; the substitute reacted with the electrolyte and the unit leaked. The recommendation was that material substitutions in critical applications require physical-properties testing before acceptance, not certification by inheritance. [LLIS 455: Nonmetallic Materials Certification](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/455)

Check: confirm the bearing lubricant, prism coatings, and thermopile potting materials on this build match the originally certified materials, with any substitution re-tested, not waved through on heritage.

### 4. Particulate contamination causing erroneous encoder or switch state signals
Loose metallic or non-metallic debris from manufacturing (weld spatter, glass, polymer) has repeatedly caused limit switches to give false state changes or lose contact. For a continuously rotating prism assembly with a position encoder and electrical contacts, the same debris source is plausible. The fix adopted was mandatory Particle Impact Noise Detection testing on all such switches before delivery. [LLIS 21: Use of Particle Impact Noise Detection Test to Detect Contamination](https://llis.nasa.gov/lesson/21)

Check: confirm PIND or equivalent contamination screening was performed on the encoder and any electrical contacts in the scan assembly, not just on the bearing/motor housing.

This is a research aid drawn from historical records, not a safety review.
